title: The Midnight Library
summary: Tomás spends pyjama night at the village library, and discovers that when the clock strikes twelve, the books do not stay still.

scenes.text:
Once a year, the village library had a pyjama night.

Don Ambrosio, the librarian, let the children bring their sleeping bags and stay until morning, among the shelves, reading by torchlight.

That year, Tomás arrived first. He had his stripy pyjamas, his torch and a bag of biscuits.

Outside it was pouring with rain. But inside, everything was warm and smelled of paper, of wood and a little bit of chocolate, because Don Ambrosio always had a mug on his desk.

They read stories until very late. Then Don Ambrosio switched off the big lights.

"Off to sleep, explorers," he said. "Books need to rest too."

But Tomás wasn't the least bit sleepy.

When everyone was asleep, he picked up his torch and tiptoed to the very back of the library. There, behind the tallest shelf, was a corner with an old rug and a little lamp. It was his favourite hiding place.

He sat down with a fat book of old maps. It had islands with strange names, hand-drawn mountains and monsters of the deep with whiskers.

He read slowly, turning over a page.

And another. And another.

Until his eyes grew heavy, and the book stayed open on his knees.

He was woken by the clock on the wall.

It gave a chime. Then another, and another. Tomás counted them under his breath: nine, ten, eleven… twelve.

And on the very last one, something wonderful happened.

A book with blue covers, on the shelf opposite, began to glow. Out from between its pages came a cloud of tiny golden sparks, swirling up into the air like a whirl of fireflies.

The book opened all by itself.

And out came first a hat. Then a boot. Then a tangled beard with two knots in it.

"Land!" shouted a gravelly voice. "Dry land at last!"

And a whole pirate sat down on the rug to dust off his sleeves.

The pirate was short, with a red nose and a parrot embroidered on his shirt.

"And who might you be, sailor?" he asked, looking at Tomás with one eye half closed.

"Tomás. And who are you?"

"Captain Quietbeard, from the blue book, chapter three!" He gave a bow. "At midnight, we characters come out to stretch our legs. Until the sun comes up. It's the oldest rule in any library."

Just then, an enormous atlas burst open, and out stepped a woman in tall boots with a leather backpack.

"Nadia, explorer of eleven deserts," she said. "And this is Fósforo."

Behind her flew a dragon the size of a cat, made entirely of paper. He sniffed Tomás, wrinkled his nose…

"Atchoo!"

And filled his hair with glitter.

"Come on," said Nadia. "We want to show you something."

They walked to the poetry shelf, the dustiest of them all. Nadia pushed three books at once, and the whole shelf swung slowly round, like a secret door, with a creak.

Behind it was a long, narrow passage, with little lamps hanging from the ceiling.

"Was this always here?" whispered Tomás.

"Always," said the captain. "Libraries are bigger on the inside than on the outside. All of them."

The walls of the passage were made of books. And from some of them came little sounds: a faraway trumpet, someone practising the piano with one finger, the hum of a busy market.

Fósforo flew ahead, lighting the way with the glitter that escaped when he breathed.

At the end of the passage was a round room, so tall you couldn't see the ceiling.

"This is where the books that hardly anyone borrows live," said Nadia, lowering her voice. "They're the most grateful of all."

There were storybooks with faded covers, recipe books full of stains and a whole encyclopaedia all about clouds.

Suddenly, Fósforo pricked up his paper ears and flew to a low shelf. He stopped in front of a small green book with soft corners.

And then they all heard it.

A very soft sound was coming from the green book. Someone was crying, very quietly, inside those pages.

Tomás crouched down and opened the green book very carefully.

On the paper appeared a girl with short hair and a yellow coat. She was holding an unlit lantern.

"Hello," said Tomás. "Why are you crying?"

"My name's Lira," she said, wiping her face on her sleeve. "And I can't finish my story."

Nadia turned the pages to the end. After chapter ten there was nothing: just a torn edge.

"Someone tore out the last pages, a very long time ago," said Lira. "I crossed the snow. I went through the forest. I learned to row. And I've been stuck here, one step from the end."

"And how did it end?" asked the captain.

"I don't know. I only know that across the water there's an island with a lighthouse. And my brother is waiting for me there. He lights the lamp every night, so I'll know which way to go."

"Then we'll find those pages," said Nadia, tightening her backpack. "Right now."

They searched the whole library. Under the rug. In the box of returned books. On the trolley of books that had got wet.

Nadia climbed the ladder on wheels to look at the highest shelves. The captain opened every drawer in Don Ambrosio's desk, asking permission out loud, just in case. Fósforo crawled behind the radiator and came out wearing a cobweb for a hat.

Nothing. Not a single one.

Lira sat down on the edge of her own story and hung her head.

"It's all right," she said quietly. "I'm used to waiting."

Nobody said anything for a long while. All you could hear was the rain outside, gentler now.

Tomás looked at Lira, at her yellow coat, at her unlit lantern. And he felt something tight in his chest.

Then an idea lit up inside him, just like a match.

"What if we write it ourselves?" he said.

Everyone turned round.

"The ending. If it won't turn up, we'll make it up. I've got a pencil in my pyjama pocket."

The captain jumped up so fast that his hat fell off.

"Can you do that?" asked Lira, her eyes very wide.

"I don't know," said Tomás. "But you didn't know how to row either, and you learned."

And then, for the first time in a hundred years, Lira let out a little laugh.

They sat in a circle around the green book.

First, Nadia drew the map: a little boat, a gentle current and an island shaped like a hat.

The captain dictated the words for the journey, because he knew everything about seas.

"Write this: and the water carried her along, unhurried, like a cradle."

Lira told Tomás what her brother's voice was like, and how he laughed, and what tune he whistled when he lit the lighthouse.

And Tomás wrote slowly, with his tongue sticking out, trying not to go over the lines.

When he had finished, Fósforo came up to the paper and blew on it, very gently, to sweep away the pencil crumbs.

When Tomás put the final full stop, the green book grew warm, like freshly baked bread.

The new words shone for a moment and then settled themselves on the paper.

And Lira looked ahead. This time, there was a way.

She climbed into a paper boat, waved with both hands and began to drift slowly away across the sea.

Far off, on an island shaped like a hat, the light of a lighthouse came on.

"Thank you!" they heard, from almost another world.

And just then, through the highest window, came the first ray of dawn.

The captain took off his hat, gave an enormous bow and climbed back into his blue book. Nadia waved goodbye and went back to her atlas. Fósforo gave Tomás a little nudge with his forehead, and flew away.

The shelves were shelves again, still and tidy.

A little while later, Tomás heard footsteps. It was Don Ambrosio, waking the children.

"Tomás! So this is where you got to."

The librarian picked the green book up off the rug. And he stood for a moment looking at the last pages, written in pencil.

He didn't say anything. Neither did Tomás.

But Don Ambrosio smiled, just a little, like someone who has known that secret for a very long time.
